The next generation

Which developments might earn a headline of their own in a future edition? Four candidates connect today’s evidence to a change that could spread across places and sectors.

Four hypotheses to keep open

Each candidate starts with an older trend. The test is whether a different mechanism gains enough reach and persistence to change decisions in several fields. The signals below could also weaken the case.

AI-driven discovery and programmable biology

Where the idea comes from

The 1990 book already anticipated an age of biology. A different proposition is that computational tools could help researchers move repeatedly between a question, a proposed design and a real-world test. McKinsey added AI for scientific discovery and engineering as a distinct domain in 2026.

What might follow

Materials, medicines and manufacturing processes could develop on shorter cycles. Access to facilities, data and independent validation would shape whose problems attract attention.

What would strengthen or weaken the case

Track independently replicated results, time to a usable product and who can afford to participate. More proposed designs alongside a stubborn validation bottleneck would weaken the case.

What changes if finding a promising material takes less time than independently testing it?

SourcesMcKinsey · Technology Trends Outlook 2026 EY · Megatrends 2020 and beyond

Physical constraints on digital progress

Where the idea comes from

Digital services make few demands on a user’s desk. Upstream they depend on electricity, grids, cooling, chips, land and investment. A national surplus of power can coexist with a long connection queue in a particular city.

What might follow

Data-centre locations and access to grid capacity could reorganise industrial geography. Residents, utilities and developers may disagree about whose use of power or water takes priority.

What would strengthen or weaken the case

Compare connection queues, local resource use and performance per unit of energy. Efficiency gains or workloads moving to less constrained places could change the trajectory.

Which digital services can a place sustain when power, water, land and grid capacity are also needed for homes and industry?

SourcesIEA · Energy and AI McKinsey · Technology Trends Outlook 2026

Economic and political activity expands into orbit

Where the idea comes from

Weather forecasting and navigation already depend on space. The candidate shift is satellite services becoming everyday dependencies for more sectors while commercial providers and states negotiate access, spectrum and the use of shared orbital space.

What might follow

A rural clinic or disaster response team can gain coverage quickly yet come to depend on a distant operator’s pricing and permissions. Space governance becomes a question about terrestrial services.

What would strengthen or weaken the case

Look for indispensable services with few substitutes, durable revenues beyond launches and workable agreements over congestion. Large investment alone would be weak evidence.

How might everyday services change when their communications, navigation or observations depend on decisions made about orbital infrastructure?

SourcesMcKinsey · Technology Trends Outlook 2026 CIFS · Megatrends 2026

The social contract is renegotiated

Where the idea comes from

Sitra’s 2026 review asks how Finland can sustain the promises of the welfare state as demographic, economic, technological and ecological conditions change. The candidate global trend is a wave of political bargains, with different answers in different places.

What might follow

Who pays for care, who bears climate losses and who owns the benefits of automation may be settled together. Public provision, commercial insurance and mutual aid could divide responsibilities differently.

What would strengthen or weaken the case

Look for durable changes in entitlements, taxation, working time and intergenerational transfers. An isolated pilot or a political slogan says little about whether a bargain will endure.

How might societies share income, care and security when paid employment and family structures change?

SourcesSitra · Towards a new social contract CSIRO · Our Future World, 2022
